identity.title: Sperm phospholipase C signaling via PLCzeta1 and PLCdelta4 is essential for Ca2+ oscillations and fertility in mice.

content.abstract: Fertilization-induced calcium (Ca2+) oscillations are essential for egg activation and embryonic development in mammals. The sperm-specific phospholipase C isoform, PLCzeta1, is the primary trigger of these oscillations. Functional and clinical studies have linked mutations or reduced expression of PLCzeta1 to male infertility. However, whether PLCzeta1 alone accounts for Ca2+ release at fertilization in all mammals remains uncertain. Male mice lacking Plczeta1 exhibit subfertility and reduced litter sizes; their sperm induce delayed, low-frequency Ca2+ oscillations, indicating a compensatory mechanism. Notably, mouse sperm express high levels of PLCdelta4, essential for completing the acrosome reaction (AR). In Plczeta1-null sperm, PLCdelta4 is upregulated and retained post-AR. These observations suggest a secondary functional role for PLCdelta4. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, we generated Plcdelta4 knockout (KO) mice. Plcdelta4-null sperm trigger attenuated, delayed Ca2+ oscillations and significantly reduced fertilization rates, indicating that PLCdelta4 contributes to but does not independently drive Ca2+ signaling. We therefore generated a Double Knockout (DKO) mouse line lacking both sperm-enriched PLCs. DKO males were sterile, with sperm failing to induce Ca2+ oscillations, and the isolated residual Ca2+ rise was insufficient to activate eggs. These findings reveal that PLCzeta1, the primary oscillator, and PLCdelta4, a compensatory factor, work cooperatively within a complex, multi-component PLC system that ensures robust fertilization. This work reveals molecular specialization among mammals in initiating the fertilization Ca2+ signals. It has implications for understanding male infertility, improving assisted reproductive technologies, and developing contraceptive strategies.
